'Thomas! Coming for marbles?'
'Yes! Wait, who's playing?'
'Me, Anju, Noor,' called Biju from the courtyard of their Kochi flats.
'I'm coming too.'
'Ah... actually, it's full today.'
'Full? It's four people. We always play four.'
Noor looked at her marbles. 'Last week you took back your blue one after you lost it. You said it was a practice round.'
'That was a joke!'
'And the week before, you moved the line.'
Thomas's ears went hot. 'When Noor lost, she gave Anju her cat's-eye. So she keeps promises, and I'm the bad one?'
'She said she'd give it. She gave it,' said Biju.
Thomas stood there, marbles clicking in his pocket. The others bent over the circle. Noor glanced up once. 'Maybe next week. If you play properly.'

qa.q: What did Noor say Thomas did with the blue marble last week?
qa.a: Noor said he took back his blue one after he lost it and called it a practice round.

qa.q: What was Thomas feeling when his ears went hot?
qa.a: He felt embarrassed and a bit angry at being left out, as the others reminded him of how he cheated.

qa.q: What could Thomas do to be invited again?
qa.a: He could play properly next week, keep his promises about marbles like Noor did, and show over a few games that he can be trusted.

qa.q: How do Biju and Noor see Thomas after the last two weeks?
qa.a: They see him as someone who doesn't keep his word in games, so they quietly leave him out, though Noor leaves a small door open.

grounding: Shows a boy quietly dropped from a marbles game after cheating, while a girl who keeps promises is trusted and kept in.

passage: I'm Chinmay, and I'm eleven. This is about the card game in our building's stairwell. Last month I peeked at Eshaan's cards when he went to drink water. I won three games in a row. I felt clever. The next Sunday, I came down with my cards and everyone was already playing. Nobody had called me. Eshaan had been called. He always gives back the cards he borrows and says sorry if he drops one. I asked, 'Can I play?' Rinku said, 'Maybe later.' Later never came. Now I know people remember. It only took one peek.

qa.a: Chinmay felt clever at first, but later felt left out and understood that people remember, when nobody called Chinmay to play.

qa.a: Chinmay could tell the others about the peek and say sorry, then play fairly every time so they slowly trust Chinmay again.

qa.a: They know Eshaan always gives back borrowed cards and says sorry, so he feels safe to play with, while Chinmay's peek made them unsure.

Class 4 teacher's note, lunch-break duty, Thursday:
For two weeks I have watched the marbles group by the neem tree. Kashish is always welcomed. When she promises 'loser gives one', she hands it over, even her favourite green one. Sachin arrived today and the children suddenly said the game was 'finished'. They started a new one as soon as he left. When I asked quietly, one child said, 'Sachin changes the rules when he's losing.' Sachin sat on the steps kicking the ground. Next, I will talk with Sachin alone, without scolding, about how the others see him and what he could do differently. I'll also keep an eye out so the group doesn't shut him out for good.

qa.a: The marbles group plays by the neem tree.

qa.q: What might Sachin be feeling as he sits on the steps kicking the ground?
qa.a: He is probably hurt and frustrated at being left out, and may not fully understand why the game suddenly 'finished'.

qa.q: What is the teacher's plan, and why is it a good choice?
qa.a: The teacher will talk with Sachin alone without scolding about how others see him, so he can learn to change, and will watch that he isn't shut out for good.

qa.q: How do the other children see Kashish compared with Sachin?
qa.a: They trust Kashish because she keeps her promises even with her favourite marble, but they avoid Sachin because he changes the rules when losing.

grounding: A teacher notes that a girl who keeps her marbles promises is always welcome while a boy who changes the rules is quietly dropped.

passage:
Saturday
Carrom on the terrace again. Bhaiya from 4B called me first. He said, "Darshan plays straight." I felt proud all day.
They didn't call Lokesh. Last Sunday he flicked the queen back with his finger when he thought nobody saw, and then said he never promised to give his turn. Everybody saw. Nobody said anything. They just stopped calling him.
Today he stood at the terrace door. Pappu said, "Board's full." It wasn't full.
I felt bad. But I also thought, one Sunday and now nobody trusts him. If I cheat once, will it be like that for me too?
Tomorrow I might ask if Lokesh can play if he promises.
Darshan

qa.a: Darshan felt proud all day, because being called first meant the others trusted Darshan to play straight.

qa.a: Asking if Lokesh can play if he promises, which offers Lokesh a way back while keeping the fair-play rule.

qa.q: What might it be like for Lokesh standing at the terrace door?

grounding: A child notices being invited to carrom for playing straight, while a friend who cheated once is quietly dropped.

passage: Behind the rice mill in the village, the boys played marbles in the dust every evening. Imran always paid what he owed. If he lost three, he dug three out of his pocket, even his favourite green one. Arnab was faster and cleverer, but twice last week he nudged his marble with his toe while the others were looking at the sky, and once he said, "I never said three, I said two." On Friday, when Imran arrived, four boys shouted, "Imran, our side!" When Arnab arrived, they went quiet and looked at their marbles. Nobody said "cheat". Nobody had to. Arnab stood at the edge, kicking a stone. By the time the mill siren went, nobody had asked him once.

qa.q: What did Imran do when he lost three marbles?
qa.a: He dug three out of his pocket, even his favourite green one.

qa.q: What might Arnab have been feeling as he kicked a stone at the edge?
qa.a: He likely felt left out and embarrassed, sensing the others no longer trusted him, even though nobody said "cheat".

qa.q: What could Arnab do to start earning back a place in the game?
qa.a: He could own up to the toe-nudges, pay what he owes, and play straight for many evenings, since trust will come back only slowly.

qa.q: How do the other boys see Imran and Arnab now?
qa.a: They see Imran as someone who keeps his word and want him on their side, while Arnab's clever play no longer counts because they can't trust him.

grounding: In a village marbles game, a boy who always pays up is welcomed while a boy who cheated a few times is quietly left out.
